claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability of near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by a kinetically frozen high-configurational-entropy state.
High configurational entropy suppresses atomic diffusion in these nanoparticles.
Local chemical fluctuations suppress atomic diffusion in these nanoparticles.
Atomic diffusion would otherwise cause phase segregation.
Atomic diffusion would otherwise cause oxidation.
High-energy rapid-shock methods are used to synthesize HEA nanoparticles.
Rapid thermal synthesis kinetically traps nanoparticles as single-phase solid solutions with randomly distributed elements.
Low-temperature solution synthesis produces a single-phase, near-equiatomic solid solution with a random atomic distribution and strong local chemical fluctuation.
Thermal annealing within the service-temperature range increases atomic mobility enough to overcome the proposed kinetic barrier.
Annealing will cause phase segregation relative to the as-synthesized baseline.
Phase segregation causes the surface elements of an HEA to cease being randomly distributed.
Annealing in an inert atmosphere will produce oxide patches and increased surface oxidation.
Annealing-induced segregation or oxidation will reduce catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
Local chemical fluctuations can alter thermoelectric behavior by disrupting long-range periodicity, scattering heat-carrying phonons, and reducing lattice thermal conductivity.
As-synthesized, rapidly cooled nanoparticles preserve a high-entropy single phase and stable catalytic or thermoelectric properties.
The proposed kinetic-trapping mechanism dominates throughout 773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric applications.
Outside the stated temperature ranges or under other atmospheres, different degradation processes may dominate.

contradictions.description: The annealing atmosphere is specified as inert to avoid extraneous oxidation, yet annealing is predicted to form oxide patches and increase surface oxidation without identifying an oxygen source.
